result.relation_rationale: The requested overall cannabis withdrawal severity is reported as the Overall withdrawal score on the 19-item Cannabis Withdrawal Scale (each item rated 0–10 for the previous 24 hours). The randomized comparison is nabiximols versus placebo. The treatment-by-time effect covers daily measurements during the 6-day medication phase (days 1–6), while the repeated-measures model includes days 1–9. All 51 randomized participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis, with missing questionnaires multiply imputed.

measurement.method: Overall severity of cannabis withdrawal measured by the 19-item Cannabis Withdrawal Scale, with each item rated 0–10 for the previous 24 hours.

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups
target.intended_effect_measure: Between-group difference in change in overall Cannabis Withdrawal Scale severity over time

reported.analysis_population: All 51 randomized participants (27 nabiximols, 24 placebo); intention-to-treat analysis; missing CWS questionnaires were multiply imputed in 5 datasets.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.

A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer. For D3.2 No, inspected context/inference or a valid scoped no-hit receipt can instead support the scoped absence of reassuring evidence; it does not assert bias occurred.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and uncertainty in inspected Evidence, scoped search receipts, or an explicit scientific limitation. Complete reading_recovery with read_pages and all context continuations. Document-structure recovery in coverage is navigation, not selected Evidence; inspect relevant unopened windows before claiming information is unreported, or retain a bounded stopping rationale. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

3|Cannabis Withdrawal
4|A Randomized Clinical Trial
5|David J. Allsop, PhD; Jan Copeland, PhD; Nicholas Lintzeris, PhD; Adrian J. Dunlop, PhD;

8|IMPORTANCE There are no medications approved for treating cannabis dependence or
9|withdrawal. The cannabis extract nabiximols (Sativex), developed as a multiple sclerosis
10|treatment, offers a potential agonist medication for cannabis withdrawal.
11|OBJECTIVE To evaluate the safety and efficacy of nabiximols in treating cannabis withdrawal.
12|DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS A 2-site, double-blind randomized clinical inpatient trial
13|with a 28-day follow-up was conducted in New South Wales, Australia. Participants included
14|51 DSM-IV-TR cannabis-dependent treatment seekers.
15|INTERVENTIONS A 6-day regimen of nabiximols (maximum daily dose, 86.4 mg of
16|Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and 80 mg of cannabidiol) or placebo with standardized
17|psychosocial interventions during a 9-day admission.
18|MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Severity of cannabis withdrawal and cravings (Cannabis
19|Withdrawal Scale), retention in withdrawal treatment, and adverse events. Secondary
20|outcomes include postwithdrawal cannabis use, health outcomes, and psychosocial
21|outcomes.
22|RESULTS Nabiximols treatment significantly reduced the overall severity of cannabis
23|withdrawal relative to placebo (F8,377.97 = 2.39; P = .01), including effects on
24|withdrawal-related irritability, depression, and cannabis cravings. Nabiximols had a more
25|limited, but still positive, therapeutic benefit on sleep disturbance, anxiety, appetite loss,
26|physical symptoms, and restlessness. Nabiximols patients remained in treatment longer
27|during medication use (unadjusted hazard ratio, 3.66 [95% CI, 1.18-11.37]; P = .02), with 2.84
28|the number needed to treat to achieve successful retention in treatment. Participants could
29|not reliably differentiate between nabiximols and placebo treatment (χ2
30|1 = 0.79; P = .67), and
31|those receiving nabiximols did not report greater intoxication (F1,6 = 0.22; P = .97). The
32|number (F1,50 = 0.3; P = .59) and severity (F1,50 = 2.69; P = .10) of adverse events did not
33|differ significantly between groups. Both groups showed reduced cannabis use at follow-up,
34|with no advantage of nabiximols over placebo for self-reported cannabis use (F1,48 = 0.29;
35|P = .75), cannabis-related problems (F1,49 = 2.33; P = .14), or cannabis dependence
36|(F1,50 < 0.01; P = .89).
37|CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In a treatment-seeking cohort, nabiximols attenuated
38|cannabis withdrawal symptoms and improved patient retention in treatment. However,
39|placebo was as effective as nabiximols in promoting long-term reductions in cannabis use
40|following medication cessation. The data support further evaluation of nabiximols for
41|management of cannabis dependence and withdrawal in treatment-seeking populations.

2|C
3|annabis is the most prevalent illicit drug in the world,1
4|and its use has been linked to a range of negative health
5|outcomes.2 Approximately 10% of cannabis users will
6|becomedependent,leadingtotreatment.3IntheUnitedStates,
7|treatment episodes involving cannabis as the primary drug in-
8|creased from 6% in 1992 to 16% in 2007.4 Cannabis was men-
9|tioned as the primary drug of concern in 287 933 episodes in
10|2007 and was one of multiple drugs of concern in almost 1 mil-
11|lion treatment episodes.4 Similar increases in cannabis treat-
12|ment seeking are observed globally.5,6 A cannabis with-
13|drawal syndrome was included for the first time in the
14|DSM-5.7,8 More than half of cannabis users report withdrawal,9
15|with primary symptoms including irritability, insomnia, de-
16|creased appetite, depressed mood, anxiety, and restlessness.10
17|Withdrawal symptoms are considered to be a major determi-
18|nant of the high relapse rates observed in individuals receiv-
19|ing treatment.11-18
20|There are no approved pharmacotherapies for managing
21|cannabis withdrawal.19-21 A range of symptomatic medica-
22|tions have been evaluated, including the antidepressants bu-
23|propion and nefazodone,22, 23 the mood stabilizers
24|divalproex24,25 and lithium,26 and the α2-adrenergic agonist
25|lofexidine,27 with limited benefits. Agonist substitution ap-
26|proaches may be more promising. Oral delivery of synthetic
27|Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC; dronabinol was the THC for-
28|mulation used) dose-dependently reduced a subset of canna-
29|bis withdrawal symptoms in laboratory24 and outpatient
30|settings.28,29Nabilone,asyntheticanalogueofTHCwithhigher
31|oral bioavailability than dronabinol, was efficacious in a re-
32|cent laboratory study.30 These findings suggest that further ex-
33|aminationofagonisttherapiesforcannabiswithdrawalarewar-
34|ranted.
35|Nabiximols (Sativex; GW Pharmaceuticals, UK) is a medi-
36|cation containing THC, cannabidiol (CBD), and various terpe-
37|noids derived from Cannabis sativa plants. It is delivered as a
38|buccal spray, with absorption through the oral mucosa, lead-
39|ing to a more predictable pharmacokinetic profile than oral
40|THC.31 The CBD content of nabiximols is of particular interest
41|given that CBD attenuates the paranoia32 and euphoria33 as-
42|sociated with THC and may have efficacy in treating anxiety,
43|depression, and psychosis.34-38 A recent case study39 re-
44|ported strong attenuation of symptoms when CBD was used
45|to treat cannabis withdrawal. Nabiximols is approved in many
46|countries to treat muscular spasticity associated with mul-
47|tiple sclerosis. Nabiximols typically produces little
48|intoxication,40 tolerance,41-43 or withdrawal.44 This indi-
49|cates low abuse potential relative to other cannabinoids, such
50|as dronabinol.45 We hypothesized that nabiximols would re-
51|duce the severity of cannabis withdrawal symptoms and in-
52|crease patient retention during inpatient detoxification, with-
53|out significant safety concerns or intoxication. Assessment of
54|cannabinoid levels in plasma and urine allowed determina-
55|tion of whether nabiximols provided effective pharmaco-
56|logicsubstitutionforcannabis.Secondaryhypotheses,thatuse
57|of nabiximols leads to reduced cannabis use and depen-
58|dence, as well as improved psychosocial outcomes at the 28-
59|day follow-up, were also tested.
60|Methods
61|Study Design
62|The study was a 2-site, randomized, double-blind, inpatient
63|trial with 6 days of nabiximols or placebo treatment, 3 days of
64|washout, and a 28-day follow-up period. Patients were admit-
65|ted for inpatient detoxification at either Sydney and Sydney
66|Eye Hospital (SSEH) or at Belmont Hospital, New South Wales,
67|Australia,betweenDecember5,2011,andOctober17,2012,with
68|follow-up completed by November 15, 2012. The trial proto-
69|col is available from the authors on request.
70|This research was approved by the Hunter New England
71|Human Research Ethics Committee. Patients gave written in-
72|formed consent to take part in the study on day 1 of admis-
73|sion to the unit, which triggered randomization. Participants
74|were compensated with A$40 for follow-up interviews.
75|Participants
76|Inclusion criteria were (1) age 18 to 65 years, (2) met criteria for
77|current DSM-IV-TR cannabis dependence with no current al-
78|cohol or other drug dependence except for nicotine and/or caf-
79|feine, (3) experienced withdrawal during previous quit at-
80|tempts, and (4) desired to reduce or quit cannabis use.
81|Exclusion criteria were (1) unstable medical or psychiatric con-
82|ditions, (2) medications initiated or dose changed in the pre-
83|vious month, (3) pregnancy, (4) urine sample negative for can-
84|nabinoids (tetrahydrocannabinol [THC]-COOH]), (5) positive
85|urine test result for other illicit substances or benzodiaz-
86|epines, or (6) received formal drug or alcohol treatment in the
87|previous month (excluding treatment for nicotine depen-
88|dence).
89|Procedures
90|Patients were referred from treatment services or responded
91|tomediaadvertisements.Eligibilityassessmentsincludedurine
92|drug screens, structured medical assessment by addiction
93|medicine specialists, and the Structured Clinical Interview for
94|DSM-IV-TR Axis I Disorders: Research Version (SCID-RV)46 by
95|a psychologist. Withdrawal, as defined by participants' expe-
96|riencing 3 or more symptoms after cessation of prolonged can-
97|nabis use or continuing use to avoid withdrawal symptoms,
98|was assessed during the SCID-RV. Race and ethnicity were
99|documented by self-report (ie, white, Aboriginal, or Torres
100|Strait Islander) for routine documentation. The study flow dia-
101|gram is presented in Figure 1.
102|Patients were requested to abstain from smoking canna-
103|bis for at least 6 hours before admission. After randomiza-
104|tion, patients completed a 6-hour orientation with baseline re-
105|searchsurveys,includingpremedicationwithdrawalmeasures
106|and detailed timeline follow-back interviews to assess canna-
107|bis use, including recent use (up to the night before admis-
108|sion). Study drugs were administered by trained nurses as per
109|protocol.

22|Psychosocial Intervention
23|A cognitive behavioral therapy-based self-completed

28|Blinding/Randomization
29|An independent statistician generated a randomization list for
30|each site using random block sizes in Stata, version 11.1 (Stata-
31|Corp) (initialization seed 675). Patients, investigators, and out-
32|come assessors were blind to treatment allocation until all re-

35|ticals, UK. The success of patient blinding was formally as-
36|sessed before hospital discharge.

39|Scale (CWS).10,18 The CWS is a 19-item scale measuring with-

58|Measurement of Plasma and Urinary Cannabinoids
59|With consent from patients, blood samples were collected on
60|day 1 (baseline, premedication), day 3 (peak dosing), and day

5|Statistical Analysis
6|Poweranalysiswasbasedonadronabinolstudy(30mg)28using
7|the Total Marijuana Withdrawal Checklist (TMWC) scores (a
8|proxy for the CWS). The analysis suggested that 20 partici-
9|pants per group would provide 99.5% power to detect a 27%
10|suppression of withdrawal with agonist treatment (mean [SD]
11|increase in TMWC score of 6.2 [1.0] from baseline to absti-
12|nence while the patient received placebo compared with an
13|increase of 4.5 [2.0] with dronabinol, using repeated-
14|measures analysis).28 Intention-to-treat analysis included all
15|51 randomized participants. For descriptive statistics, group
16|differencesincontinuousvariablesused2-wayanalysesofvari-
17|ance, and categorical variables used Pearson χ2 or Fisher ex-
18|act test when cells had a count of less than 5. Statistical analy-
19|ses were performed with SPSS, version 21 (SPSS Corp).
20|The primary analysis compared main effects and the in-
21|teraction of treatment and time on mean difference from base-
22|line CWS scores in a mixed models for repeated measures re-
23|gression with first-order autoregressive covariance
24|structure.64-66 The model was adjusted with covariates known
25|or suspected to influence the experience of cannabis with-
26|drawal (SDS scores),10,18 baseline variables that were signifi-
27|cantly different between groups (CWS scores and Sheehan Dis-
28|ability Scale scores), and other possible moderators of
29|withdrawal (use of NRT/cigarettes,67 temazepam, and caf-
30|feine during abstinence).
31|Post hoc pairwise comparisons compared withdrawal be-
32|tween groups on each day of treatment adjusted for multiple
33|comparisonsusingtheBonferronimethod.Hierarchicalmodel
34|building (step 1: time, treatment, time × treatment; step 2: ad-
35|dition of covariates) explored changes in variance explained
36|using pseudo-R2 calculated from log-likelihood ratios (R2
37|LR).68
38|Akaike information criteria69 calculated model fit (smaller val-
39|ues indicate better fit). Separate analyses tested the effect of
40|nabiximols on attenuating DSM-5 cannabis withdrawal symp-
41|toms (Supplement [eTable 1]).7 Effect sizes are reported using
42|the bias-corrected Hedges g (raw difference between 2 means
43|divided by SD adjusted for population size).70 Parametric sta-
44|tistics were used on Likert data because interval structure can
45|be assumed if scales are presented as symmetrical.71 Residu-
46|als from the primary withdrawal efficacy analysis were nor-
47|mally distributed.
48|The effect of nabiximols on retention in withdrawal treat-
49|ment was assessed with a stepwise Cox proportional hazards
50|regression model, first looking at treatment alone, then con-
51|trolling for SDS, Sheehan Disability Scale, and CWS scores and
52|the use of NRT/cigarettes, temazepam, and caffeine. The pro-
53|portions of people in each treatment group reporting each AE
54|were analyzed using χ2 or the Fisher exact test. Time to re-
55|lapse between the end of the inpatient stay and the 28-day fol-
56|low-up were assessed using a Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.
57|Finally, changes in cannabis-related problems, the severity of
58|cannabis dependence, and cannabis use levels were assessed
59|using the mixed models for repeated measures approach. All
60|tests were 2-sided, with significance set at P ≤.05.
61|Results
62|Demographics and Clinical Features
63|A total of 51 patients were randomized to receive placebo
64|(n = 24) or nabiximols (n = 27). Patients reported high levels
65|of cannabis use (mean [SD], 22.98 [20.66] g/wk),49 corrobo-
66|rated by day 1 urine (Supplement [eFigure 1]) and plasma
67|(Supplement [eFigure 2]) THC and THC-COOH levels. Pa-
68|tients had smoked cannabis for 20.43 (9.22) years, and their
69|mean score of 12.04 (2.71) on the 15-point SDS scale indicated
70|severe cannabis dependence (Table 1). Groups were well
71|matched apart from differences in baseline CWS and Shee-
72|han Disability Scale scores (Table 1). The Sheehan Disability
73|Scale scores were also significantly different between study
74|sites.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

This is a question about baseline imbalance suggesting a randomization problem, not about how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed. Do not use the baseline table to backfill either process question.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

In addition, nabiximols signifi- cantly reduced cravings, irritability, and depression. Anxiety and cravings fell below pretreatment baseline levels in both groups during treatment, possibly resulting from high base- line anxiety associated with imminent inpatient detoxifica- tion and a lack of cannabis-related cues in the inpatient envi- ronment. Nabiximols as an Agonist Replacement Therapy During
Cannabis Withdrawal
A Randomized Clinical Trial
David J. Allsop, PhD; Jan Copeland, PhD; Nicholas Lintzeris, PhD; Adrian J. Dunlop, PhD;
Mark Montebello, FAChAM; Craig Sadler, FAChAM; Gonzalo R. Rivas, BNurs; Rohan M. Holland, BNurs;
Peter Muhleisen, BPharm, MPSA; Melissa M. Norberg, PhD; Jessica Booth, BSc (Hons); Iain S. McGregor, PhD
IMPORTANCE There are no medications approved for treating cannabis dependence or
withdrawal. The cannabis extract nabiximols (Sativex), developed as a multiple sclerosis
treatment, offers a potential agonist medication for cannabis withdrawal.
OBJECTIVE To evaluate the safety and efficacy of nabiximols in treating cannabis withdrawal.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS A 2-site, double-blind randomized clinical inpatient trial
with a 28-day follow-up was conducted in New South Wales, Australia. Participants included
51 DSM-IV-TR cannabis-dependent treatment seekers.
INTERVENTIONS A 6-day regimen of nabiximols (maximum daily dose, 86.4 mg of
Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and 80 mg of cannabidiol) or placebo with standardized
psychosocial interventions during a 9-day admission.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Severity of cannabis withdrawal and cravings (Cannabis
Withdrawal Scale), retention in withdrawal treatment, and adverse events. Secondary
outcomes include postwithdrawal cannabis use, health outcomes, and psychosocial
outcomes.
RESULTS Nabiximols treatment significantly reduced the overall severity of cannabis
withdrawal relative to placebo (F8,377.97 = 2.39; P = .01), including effects on
withdrawal-related irritability, depression, and cannabis cravings. Nabiximols had a more
limited, but still positive, therapeutic benefit on sleep disturbance, anxiety, appetite loss,
physical symptoms, and restlessness. Nabiximols patients remained in treatment longer
during medication use (unadjusted hazard ratio, 3.66 [95% CI, 1.18-11.37]; P = .02), with 2.84
the number needed to treat to achieve successful retention in treatment. Participants could
not reliably differentiate between nabiximols and placebo treatment (χ2
1 = 0.79; P = .67), and
those receiving nabiximols did not report greater intoxication (F1,6 = 0.22; P = .97). The
number (F1,50 = 0.3; P = .59) and severity (F1,50 = 2.69; P = .10) of adverse events did not
differ significantly between groups. Both groups showed reduced cannabis use at follow-up,
with no advantage of nabiximols over placebo for self-reported cannabis use (F1,48 = 0.29;
P = .75), cannabis-related problems (F1,49 = 2.33; P = .14), or cannabis dependence
(F1,50 < 0.01; P = .89).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In a treatment-seeking cohort, nabiximols attenuated
cannabis withdrawal symptoms and improved patient retention in treatment. However,
placebo was as effective as nabiximols in promoting long-term reductions in cannabis use
following medication cessation. The data support further evaluation of nabiximols for
management of cannabis dependence and withdrawal in treatment-seeking populations.

2|nabiximols were best assessed initially in an inpatient setting
3|withoutconfoundersofconcurrentillicitcannabisorotherdrug
4|use. The focus on heavy users reporting past cannabis with-
5|drawal effects limits the generalizability of findings to popu-
6|lations of lighter users. Randomization did not distribute pa-
7|tients equally with respect to baseline withdrawal or Sheehan
8|Disability Scale scores, although both were included as covar-
9|iates in analyses to minimize the bias arising from these dis-
10|crepancies. Axis II comorbidity was not assessed. Despite sta-
11|tistical correction for the use of temazepam, administration
12|of sleep medications will have disrupted the magnitude of
13|withdrawal-related sleep difficulties. Use of other psychotro-
14|pic medications (eg, antidepressants) may also influence with-
15|drawal symptoms, although the use of such medications was
16|balanced by randomization (Author Table 4).
17|Conclusions
18|Thisstudysupportstheuseofnabiximolsasanagonisttherapy
19|for reducing the severity and time course of cannabis with-
20|drawal and for retaining participants in withdrawal treat-
21|ment. Nabiximols significantly suppressed withdrawal-
22|related irritability (among the most severe and clinically
23|significantsymptomsintheoutpatientsetting),10cravings,and
24|depression. However, nabiximols was no more effective than
25|placebo in encouraging long-term reductions in cannabis use.
26|The follow-up outcomes may not be surprising given that the
27|design used was akin to an unassisted relapse prevention
28|model, and there is little precedence for medication-assisted
29|withdrawal to affect long-term abstinence without ongoing
30|support. These findings, however, identify a promising ap-
31|proach for cannabis withdrawal management and strengthen
32|the case for agonist substitution medication for cannabis with-
33|drawal. A direct comparison of nabiximols with other canna-
34|binoid agonists (dronabinol or nabilone) may be of interest in
35|the future to test whether the THC-CBD combination has ad-
36|ditional therapeutic benefits over THC alone.

8|Cannabinoid plasma analysis
9|Cannabinoids were extracted from 0.5 mL plasma samples using Styre Screen® SSTHC063 solid phase extraction
10|columns (60 mg/3 mL) from United Chemical Technologies (PA, USA) as per manufacturer instructions. Briefly, 2 mL
11|cold acetonitrile was added to each sample to precipitate plasma proteins. The supernatant was aspirated following
12|centrifugation, reduced to 200 uL using a vacuum concentrator and diluted to 2 mL with distilled water. The diluted
13|sample was loaded directly onto the column, washed with 1 mL Water/Acetonitrile/Ammonia (84:15:1), dried under
14|vacuum and eluted with 3 mL Hexane/Ethyl Acetate/Glacial Acetic Acid (49:49:2). Extracts were dried under nitrogen
15|at 60oC and reconstituted in 50μL initial mobile phase (40% methanol and 60% 10 mM ammonium acetate) for analysis.
16|Chromatographic separation was performed on a Pinnacle DB Biphenyl column (100 mm x 2.1 mm, 1.9 μm) from
17|Restek Inc (PA, USA) via gradient elution at 0.3 mL/min using a Shimadzu NexeraTM ultra high performance liquid
18|chromatograph (Shimadzu Corp, Kyoto, Japan). Analyte and internal standard ion transitions were acquired via
19|multiple reaction monitoring using a Shimadzu 8030 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer operated in positive
20|atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation mode. Cannabinoid standards obtained from Cerilliant® (TX, USA) were
21|diluted to yield stock solutions for calibrator and quality control (QC) sample preparation. Drug-free human plasma
22|(Australian Red Cross Blood Service, NSW, Australia) was fortified with stock solution to form calibrators and QC
23|samples covering concentration ranges 1-40 ng/mL for CBD, 0.5-20 ng/mL for THC, 5-200 ng/mL for THC COOH and
24|2.5-100 ng/mL for 11OH THC. The limits of quantification were 1.5, 0.5, 5 and 4 ng/mL, respectively.

result.relation_rationale: The requested overall cannabis withdrawal severity is reported as the Overall withdrawal score on the 19-item Cannabis Withdrawal Scale (each item rated 0–10 for the previous 24 hours). The randomized comparison is nabiximols versus placebo. The treatment-by-time effect covers daily measurements during the 6-day medication phase (days 1–6), while the repeated-measures model includes days 1–9. All 51 randomized participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis, with missing questionnaires multiply imputed.

measurement.method: Overall severity of cannabis withdrawal measured by the 19-item Cannabis Withdrawal Scale, with each item rated 0–10 for the previous 24 hours.

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups
target.intended_effect_measure: Between-group difference in change in overall Cannabis Withdrawal Scale severity over time

reported.analysis_population: All 51 randomized participants (27 nabiximols, 24 placebo); intention-to-treat analysis; missing CWS questionnaires were multiply imputed in 5 datasets.

questions.wording: Were participants aware of their assigned intervention during the trial?
questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

sections.excerpt: If carers or people delivering the interventions are aware of the assigned intervention then its implementation, or administration of non-protocol interventions, may differ between the intervention groups. Blinding may prevent such differences. If randomized allocation was not concealed, then it is likely that carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of participants’ assigned intervention during the trial.

sections.excerpt: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.4

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
sections.excerpt: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

Nabiximols as an Agonist Replacement Therapy During
Cannabis Withdrawal
A Randomized Clinical Trial
David J. Allsop, PhD; Jan Copeland, PhD; Nicholas Lintzeris, PhD; Adrian J. Dunlop, PhD;
Mark Montebello, FAChAM; Craig Sadler, FAChAM; Gonzalo R. Rivas, BNurs; Rohan M. Holland, BNurs;
Peter Muhleisen, BPharm, MPSA; Melissa M. Norberg, PhD; Jessica Booth, BSc (Hons); Iain S. McGregor, PhD
IMPORTANCE There are no medications approved for treating cannabis dependence or
withdrawal. The cannabis extract nabiximols (Sativex), developed as a multiple sclerosis
treatment, offers a potential agonist medication for cannabis withdrawal.
OBJECTIVE To evaluate the safety and efficacy of nabiximols in treating cannabis withdrawal.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS A 2-site, double-blind randomized clinical inpatient trial
with a 28-day follow-up was conducted in New South Wales, Australia. Participants included
51 DSM-IV-TR cannabis-dependent treatment seekers.
INTERVENTIONS A 6-day regimen of nabiximols (maximum daily dose, 86.4 mg of
Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and 80 mg of cannabidiol) or placebo with standardized
psychosocial interventions during a 9-day admission.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Severity of cannabis withdrawal and cravings (Cannabis
Withdrawal Scale), retention in withdrawal treatment, and adverse events. Secondary
outcomes include postwithdrawal cannabis use, health outcomes, and psychosocial
outcomes.
RESULTS Nabiximols treatment significantly reduced the overall severity of cannabis
withdrawal relative to placebo (F8,377.97 = 2.39; P = .01), including effects on
withdrawal-related irritability, depression, and cannabis cravings. Nabiximols had a more
limited, but still positive, therapeutic benefit on sleep disturbance, anxiety, appetite loss,
physical symptoms, and restlessness. Nabiximols patients remained in treatment longer
during medication use (unadjusted hazard ratio, 3.66 [95% CI, 1.18-11.37]; P = .02), with 2.84
the number needed to treat to achieve successful retention in treatment. Participants could
not reliably differentiate between nabiximols and placebo treatment (χ2
1 = 0.79; P = .67), and
those receiving nabiximols did not report greater intoxication (F1,6 = 0.22; P = .97). The
number (F1,50 = 0.3; P = .59) and severity (F1,50 = 2.69; P = .10) of adverse events did not
differ significantly between groups. Both groups showed reduced cannabis use at follow-up,
with no advantage of nabiximols over placebo for self-reported cannabis use (F1,48 = 0.29;
P = .75), cannabis-related problems (F1,49 = 2.33; P = .14), or cannabis dependence
(F1,50 < 0.01; P = .89).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In a treatment-seeking cohort, nabiximols attenuated
cannabis withdrawal symptoms and improved patient retention in treatment. However,
placebo was as effective as nabiximols in promoting long-term reductions in cannabis use
following medication cessation. The data support further evaluation of nabiximols for
management of cannabis dependence and withdrawal in treatment-seeking populations.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.

A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer. For D3.2 No, inspected context/inference or a valid scoped no-hit receipt can instead support the scoped absence of reassuring evidence; it does not assert bias occurred.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

Nabiximols as an Agonist Replacement Therapy During
Cannabis Withdrawal
A Randomized Clinical Trial
David J. Allsop, PhD; Jan Copeland, PhD; Nicholas Lintzeris, PhD; Adrian J. Dunlop, PhD;
Mark Montebello, FAChAM; Craig Sadler, FAChAM; Gonzalo R. Rivas, BNurs; Rohan M. Holland, BNurs;
Peter Muhleisen, BPharm, MPSA; Melissa M. Norberg, PhD; Jessica Booth, BSc (Hons); Iain S. McGregor, PhD
IMPORTANCE There are no medications approved for treating cannabis dependence or
withdrawal. The cannabis extract nabiximols (Sativex), developed as a multiple sclerosis
treatment, offers a potential agonist medication for cannabis withdrawal.
OBJECTIVE To evaluate the safety and efficacy of nabiximols in treating cannabis withdrawal.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS A 2-site, double-blind randomized clinical inpatient trial
with a 28-day follow-up was conducted in New South Wales, Australia. Participants included
51 DSM-IV-TR cannabis-dependent treatment seekers.
INTERVENTIONS A 6-day regimen of nabiximols (maximum daily dose, 86.4 mg of
Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and 80 mg of cannabidiol) or placebo with standardized
psychosocial interventions during a 9-day admission.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Severity of cannabis withdrawal and cravings (Cannabis
Withdrawal Scale), retention in withdrawal treatment, and adverse events. Secondary
outcomes include postwithdrawal cannabis use, health outcomes, and psychosocial
outcomes.
RESULTS Nabiximols treatment significantly reduced the overall severity of cannabis
withdrawal relative to placebo (F8,377.97 = 2.39; P = .01), including effects on
withdrawal-related irritability, depression, and cannabis cravings. Nabiximols had a more
limited, but still positive, therapeutic benefit on sleep disturbance, anxiety, appetite loss,
physical symptoms, and restlessness. Nabiximols patients remained in treatment longer
during medication use (unadjusted hazard ratio, 3.66 [95% CI, 1.18-11.37]; P = .02), with 2.84
the number needed to treat to achieve successful retention in treatment. Participants could
not reliably differentiate between nabiximols and placebo treatment (χ2
1 = 0.79; P = .67), and
those receiving nabiximols did not report greater intoxication (F1,6 = 0.22; P = .97). The
number (F1,50 = 0.3; P = .59) and severity (F1,50 = 2.69; P = .10) of adverse events did not
differ significantly between groups. Both groups showed reduced cannabis use at follow-up,
with no advantage of nabiximols over placebo for self-reported cannabis use (F1,48 = 0.29;
P = .75), cannabis-related problems (F1,49 = 2.33; P = .14), or cannabis dependence
(F1,50 < 0.01; P = .89).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In a treatment-seeking cohort, nabiximols attenuated
cannabis withdrawal symptoms and improved patient retention in treatment. However,
placebo was as effective as nabiximols in promoting long-term reductions in cannabis use
following medication cessation. The data support further evaluation of nabiximols for
management of cannabis dependence and withdrawal in treatment-seeking populations.

answers.justification: Report states 14.4% missing data from baseline through day 7, the first medication-free day, and 28.6% through day 9; missing questionnaires were multiply imputed. Thus availability for the CWS endpoint over the approved treatment window was not shown for nearly all randomized participants, despite ITT inclusion. Arm-specific observed counts during days 1–6 are not given, limiting precision.
unknowns: Arm-specific count of observed CWS questionnaires during the treatment days and missing values by time.

counterevidence.implication: All randomized participants were included in the analysis and missing questionnaires were multiply imputed, which retains the assignment population but does not make missing observations observed.

answers.justification: The report used multiple imputation after noting 14.4% then 28.6% missingness, but reports no sensitivity analysis spanning plausible missing-outcome values or other bias-correcting method. The Little test is described as assessing MCAR and is non-significant; it does not itself establish robustness to plausible departures.
unknowns: Imputation model predictors and sensitivity of the CWS effect to plausible missingness mechanisms.

answers.justification: Most missingness consisted of whole CWS questionnaires due to early dropout. Because withdrawal severity is the outcome, symptom severity could plausibly relate to dropout; however the source does not establish this linkage for individuals. Little's test (p=.89) did not reject MCAR, which counterbalances but does not prove missingness unrelated to true severity.
unknowns: Whether early dropout was driven by participants' withdrawal severity or unrelated dissatisfaction with the inpatient setting.

counterevidence.implication: The reported MCAR test was non-significant (p=.89), providing some counterpoint to outcome-dependent missingness, but cannot confirm the missingness mechanism.

answers.justification: Though outcome-dependent missingness is possible, the report does not provide reasons by participant/arm or relate early dropout to withdrawal status; its MCAR test did not reject MCAR. Those facts do not justify saying dependence likely, nor do they establish absence of such dependence.
unknowns: Whether withdrawal scores or prognosis differed among early dropouts and completers.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.

A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer. For D3.2 No, inspected context/inference or a valid scoped no-hit receipt can instead support the scoped absence of reassuring evidence; it does not assert bias occurred.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and uncertainty in inspected Evidence, scoped search receipts, or an explicit scientific limitation. Complete reading_recovery with read_pages and all context continuations. Document-structure recovery in coverage is navigation, not selected Evidence; inspect relevant unopened windows before claiming information is unreported, or retain a bounded stopping rationale. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.excerpt: Comparable methods of outcome measurement involve the same measurement methods and thresholds, used at comparable time points. sections.excerpt: Knowledge of the assigned intervention could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement, and intervention provider decision outcomes. They are unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes that do not involve judgement, for example all-cause mortality.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.5
sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which knowledge of intervention status could have influenced outcome assessment but there is no reason to believe that it did from those in which knowledge of intervention status was likely to influence outcome assessment. When there are strong levels of belief in either beneficial or harmful effects of the intervention, it is more likely that the outcome was influenced.

answer_anchors.text: Measurement or ascertainment could differ between intervention groups.
The same comparable measurement or ascertainment was used between groups.

questions.bias_construct: Whether measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between intervention groups.
considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.

Tie every monitoring difference to the approved event. Extra visits for toxicity monitoring do not establish differential measurement of mortality when death is captured through the same complete registry in both groups; those same visits may change detection of a lab-detected toxicity measured at those visits. State any mortality-specific pathway if one is supported.

For adverse events, compare the actual start and end of the AE observation window, visit schedule, post-treatment follow-up, and ascertainment method with the approved safety window. Treatment duration, median progression-free survival, or a treatment-emergent label alone does not establish when or how adverse events were observed.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when comparability of measurement or ascertainment cannot be assessed.
questions.official_guidance: Comparable methods of outcome measurement involve the same measurement methods and thresholds, used at comparable time points. Differences between intervention groups may arise because of ‘diagnostic detection bias’ in the context of passive collection of outcome data, or if an intervention involves additional visits to a healthcare provider.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome assessors were aware of the intervention received, when 4.1 and 4.2 are not yes/probably yes. Identify the assessor's identity and role: who determines the approved outcome at the relevant time point, not merely who records it.
considerations: The assessor can be a participant, intervention provider, or independent observer.

This asks only whether the relevant assessor knew assignment. It does not establish that the measurement was susceptible to bias, that detection opportunities differed, or that knowledge likely changed the assessment; those are separate questions.
Unknown assessor identity or awareness does not prevent conditional reasoning about whether the measurement could be influenced if awareness existed.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when the outcome assessor was blinded to intervention status. For participant-reported outcomes, the participant is the outcome assessor, so participant blinding can determine this answer. This question is applicable only after the stated activation conditions.
evidence_needed: Who assessed the outcome and whether that assessor was blinded to intervention status.
invalid_shortcuts: participant blinding without identifying the outcome assessor
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when assessor awareness cannot be determined; do not infer blinding from an objective endpoint or from blinding elsewhere in the trial.

answer_anchors.text: Knowledge of intervention could influence assessment.
The outcome assessment could not be influenced by knowledge of intervention.

questions.bias_construct: Whether assessment could have been influenced by knowledge of intervention received. Keep assessor awareness separate from the mechanism by which awareness could change a judgement.
considerations: Assess whether knowledge could influence this outcome. Evidence that influence actually occurred belongs to 4.5; its absence does not resolve 4.4.

Possible influence requires a judgement or reporting pathway through which assessor awareness could matter. Awareness alone is not a measurement difference, and a susceptible outcome does not by itself show that influence was possible in this assessment.
When a composite mixes objective and subjective components, assess each component's pathway separately and retain uncertainty where a component-specific link is unresolved.
questions.decision_rule: Knowledge could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving judgement, and intervention-provider decisions; it is unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes without judgement, such as all-cause mortality. A standardized instrument does not remove judgment from elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment.
evidence_needed: Outcome type, assessor role, degree of judgement, and whether knowledge of assignment could change assessment.
invalid_shortcuts: participant blinding without identifying the outcome assessor
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when possible influence cannot be determined; this question is conditional on awareness in 4.3.
questions.official_guidance: Knowledge of the assigned intervention could influence participant-reported outcomes, observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement, and intervention provider decision outcomes. They are unlikely to influence observer-reported outcomes that do not involve judgement, for example all-cause mortality.

questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 4.3: Could assessment of the outcome have been influenced by knowledge of intervention received?

answer_anchors.text: Knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.
Knowledge could have influenced assessment but it was not likely to do so.

questions.bias_construct: Whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced outcome assessment. Require evidence or strong beliefs plus a judgement opportunity; awareness alone does not establish influence.
considerations: Possible influence without evidence it occurred maps differently from likely influence.

Likely influence requires more than assessor awareness or a possible pathway: look for evidence it occurred, or strong beliefs and a real judgement opportunity. Keep this conclusion separate from measurement susceptibility and detection opportunity.
Objective components can provide valid reassurance for those components without overriding likely influence or unresolved Evidence for subjective components in the same Result.
questions.decision_rule: Distinguish possible influence without reason to believe it occurred from likely influence. Strong beliefs about benefits or harms make influence more likely, for example patient-reported symptoms or recovery assessed by an intervention provider. A standardized scale or grading rule does not by itself remove an elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment pathway.
evidence_needed: Evidence of actual influence or strong beliefs and judgement opportunities that make influence likely, given the assessor and outcome.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of influence cannot be judged; this question is conditional on possible influence in 4.4.

When there are strong levels of belief in either beneficial or harmful effects of the intervention, it is more likely that the outcome was influenced.

Nabiximols as an Agonist Replacement Therapy During
Cannabis Withdrawal
A Randomized Clinical Trial
David J. Allsop, PhD; Jan Copeland, PhD; Nicholas Lintzeris, PhD; Adrian J. Dunlop, PhD;
Mark Montebello, FAChAM; Craig Sadler, FAChAM; Gonzalo R. Rivas, BNurs; Rohan M. Holland, BNurs;
Peter Muhleisen, BPharm, MPSA; Melissa M. Norberg, PhD; Jessica Booth, BSc (Hons); Iain S. McGregor, PhD
IMPORTANCE There are no medications approved for treating cannabis dependence or
withdrawal. The cannabis extract nabiximols (Sativex), developed as a multiple sclerosis
treatment, offers a potential agonist medication for cannabis withdrawal.
OBJECTIVE To evaluate the safety and efficacy of nabiximols in treating cannabis withdrawal.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS A 2-site, double-blind randomized clinical inpatient trial
with a 28-day follow-up was conducted in New South Wales, Australia. Participants included
51 DSM-IV-TR cannabis-dependent treatment seekers.
INTERVENTIONS A 6-day regimen of nabiximols (maximum daily dose, 86.4 mg of
Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol and 80 mg of cannabidiol) or placebo with standardized
psychosocial interventions during a 9-day admission.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Severity of cannabis withdrawal and cravings (Cannabis
Withdrawal Scale), retention in withdrawal treatment, and adverse events. Secondary
outcomes include postwithdrawal cannabis use, health outcomes, and psychosocial
outcomes.
RESULTS Nabiximols treatment significantly reduced the overall severity of cannabis
withdrawal relative to placebo (F8,377.97 = 2.39; P = .01), including effects on
withdrawal-related irritability, depression, and cannabis cravings. Nabiximols had a more
limited, but still positive, therapeutic benefit on sleep disturbance, anxiety, appetite loss,
physical symptoms, and restlessness. Nabiximols patients remained in treatment longer
during medication use (unadjusted hazard ratio, 3.66 [95% CI, 1.18-11.37]; P = .02), with 2.84
the number needed to treat to achieve successful retention in treatment. Participants could
not reliably differentiate between nabiximols and placebo treatment (χ2
1 = 0.79; P = .67), and
those receiving nabiximols did not report greater intoxication (F1,6 = 0.22; P = .97). The
number (F1,50 = 0.3; P = .59) and severity (F1,50 = 2.69; P = .10) of adverse events did not
differ significantly between groups. Both groups showed reduced cannabis use at follow-up,
with no advantage of nabiximols over placebo for self-reported cannabis use (F1,48 = 0.29;
P = .75), cannabis-related problems (F1,49 = 2.33; P = .14), or cannabis dependence
(F1,50 < 0.01; P = .89).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In a treatment-seeking cohort, nabiximols attenuated
cannabis withdrawal symptoms and improved patient retention in treatment. However,
placebo was as effective as nabiximols in promoting long-term reductions in cannabis use
following medication cessation. The data support further evaluation of nabiximols for
management of cannabis dependence and withdrawal in treatment-seeking populations.

questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish protocol or ethics approval, plan finalization, amendment effective dates, registry posting or update, data cutoff, database lock, and investigators' access to unblinded outcome data; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis. Capture each dated event as reported; approval, cutoff, or database lock does not by itself establish when investigators could see unblinded outcomes.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An SAP embedded in a protocol, supplement, or combined document is still plan Evidence when its section and scope can be located; a separate SAP file is not required. An absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data. Protocol approval, ethics approval, amendment, initial registry posting, registry update, retrieval, data cutoff, and database lock are distinct events; none substitutes for the source-located date of plan finalization or investigator access to unblinded results.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent. A data cutoff or database lock is not itself proof of when investigators accessed unblinded outcomes. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results. Not establishing that a plan was early is not evidence that it was late: ground a negative chronology inference in source facts and trial circumstances, or preserve no_information when those cannot support a reasonable probable answer.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; a source-located finalization date before investigator access differs from the same plan with access timing unresolved.

A plan may be an identified section of a combined protocol or supplement. Navigate to that section and retain its exact Source and page coordinates; the lack of a separately named SAP file does not show that no plan exists.

Distinguish confidential data-monitoring access from access by trial investigators making analysis decisions. Staff providing confidential data to a monitoring committee are excepted in the official guidance; that access alone does not establish late prespecification. Public interim results are different evidence. Refining an analysis with blinded data is generally acceptable unless variables reveal intervention identity.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.

A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
